item.dc:creator: Elizabeth Agboola
item.content:encoded: Have you ever spent six hours in an airport waiting for your connecting flight, watching the departure screens, browsing duty-free shops and wondering what the city outside looks like? Perhaps you were connecting through Istanbul, Doha, Dubai or Addis Ababa. You were technically in another country, but the closest you came to experiencing it was buying a souvenir at the airport. What if I told you that some airlines could help you turn that connection into an additional holiday, sometimes even providing accommodation? Having travelled to more than 70 countries, I have learnt that one of the smartest ways to travel is to pay attention to the journey, not just the destination. Many Nigerians book international tickets based on price, travel time and baggage allowance. These are important considerations, but there is another question worth asking: What else can this ticket give me? I am talking about stopovers, not the hurried two-hour connection where you are running between terminals, but an intentional break in your journey that allows you to experience another destination before continuing to the country you originally planned to visit. And with the right airline, itinerary and travel documents, that additional experience might cost less than you imagine. First, Understand What You Are Booking A layover is generally a connection between flights; a stopover is a longer, planned break in your journey. Airlines define these differently, and the distinction matters because some offer special hotel packages, sightseeing tours or complimentary accommodation to qualifying passengers. For example, imagine travelling from Lagos to London through Istanbul. Instead of spending a few hours at Istanbul Airport, you could investigate whether your ticket qualifies for a longer stopover, allowing you to explore Istanbul before continuing to London. You have now turned one international journey into an opportunity to experience two destinations outside Nigeria. The secret is to investigate the stopover before purchasing your ticket, rather than arriving at the airport and hoping the airline will allow you to stay longer. Turkish Airlines: Turn Istanbul Into Part of Your Holiday Turkish Airlines operates a Stopover in Istanbul programme for eligible international passengers connecting through Istanbul Airport. For visa purposes, Nigerians do not qualify, but with a valid Turkish visa you would be able to qualify for some of the perks. Qualifying travellers with connections of at least 20 hours and up to seven days may receive complimentary hotel accommodation. Under the standard programme, eligible Economy Class passengers can receive one night in a four-star hotel, while Business Class passengers may receive two nights in a five-star or boutique hotel. Imagine travelling from Abuja or Lagos through Istanbul to London, Paris or another European destination. Rather than treating Istanbul as somewhere you simply change planes, you could plan time to experience the Grand Bazaar, the Bosphorus and the city’s extraordinary cultural heritage. The programme has specific conditions, including qualifying return tickets, participating countries of departure and an application made at least 72 hours before the relevant flight. The complimentary accommodation does not cover every expense. Airport transfers, visa fees and other personal costs remain your responsibility. And for Nigerian passport holders, permission to enter Türkiye must be established before departure. A hotel voucher is not a substitute for a visa. There is also Touristanbul, a separate complimentary sightseeing programme for eligible passengers with shorter connections, typically between six and 24 hours. The two programmes have different conditions and cannot simply be combined. Qatar Airways: A Stopover That Requires More Planning Qatar Airways offers an opportunity to turn a connection through Doha into an additional holiday. However, for Nigerian passport holders, there is an important distinction between the airline’s advertised stopover offers and the actual requirements for entering Qatar. While Qatar Airways promotes discounted stopover accommodation, Nigerian travellers should not assume they can access these packages without first satisfying Qatar’s visa requirements. Under the arrangement applicable to Nigerian travellers, obtaining the relevant visa requires purchasing an eligible Discover Qatar package with a minimum of three nights’ accommodation from accredited travel companies in Nigeria. This means the stopover is not necessarily an opportunity to enjoy complimentary or heavily discounted accommodation. Instead, its value lies in the possibility of incorporating Doha into an international journey without purchasing an entirely separate return flight from Nigeria. For example, if you are travelling from Lagos to Singapore through Doha, you could investigate a ticket that allows you to spend three nights in Qatar before continuing to Singapore. You would still need to budget for the qualifying Discover Qatar accommodation package, visa requirements, meals, activities and other expenses. The potential saving is therefore in the flight arrangement rather than the hotel. This is an important lesson about stopover programmes: what an airline advertises globally may not be equally accessible to every passport holder . Before booking, confirm your visa eligibility, the required Discover Qatar package and whether the extended stopover changes your airfare. Ethiopian Airlines: Discover Addis Ababa on Your Way to Another Destination For travellers heading to destinations across Africa and beyond, Ethiopian Airlines offers an opportunity worth investigating. Eligible passengers connecting through Addis Ababa for between eight and 24 hours on qualifying Ethiopian Airlines tickets can receive complimentary hotel accommodation, meals and airport transfers. The airline also offers sightseeing experiences through Ethiopian Holidays. Imagine flying from Abuja to Cape Town through Addis Ababa. Instead of spending a long connection inside the airport, you could use an eligible stopover to experience Ethiopian coffee culture, local cuisine and some of the capital’s attractions before continuing to South Africa. The airline generally issues accommodation vouchers to qualifying passengers at their departure airport or transit desk (but make sure you already have your visa before going to the desk). Passengers wishing to leave the airport must still satisfy Ethiopia’s entry requirements. The airline may assist with transit documentation under its qualifying programme, but this should be confirmed before travel. For me, this is an excellent example of how a journey through Africa can become an opportunity to discover more of the continent. Emirates: Understand the Difference Between Dubai Connect and a Dubai Holiday Dubai is already a familiar destination to many Nigerian travellers, but there is an important distinction between deliberately stopping in Dubai and qualifying for Emirates’ Dubai Connect service. Dubai Connect can provide accommodation and other transit assistance to eligible passengers with qualifying connections, generally between six and 26 hours. However, it is designed around the best available flight connection, not simply a passenger’s desire to extend a holiday. If you deliberately choose a much longer connection when a shorter eligible one exists, you may not qualify for the complimentary service. That does not mean you cannot plan Dubai into a wider holiday. You can investigate a paid multi-city itinerary or a ticket that allows a longer stay. UAE government is also constantly changing its rules, so make sure to check all this properly before booking that trip. For example, you might arrange Lagos to Dubai, spend several nights there, then continue to Bangkok or Singapore before returning home. But that is a planned multi-city journey, not necessarily a free airline s

item.title: 10 things that worry me about chasing the 2027 total solar eclipse in Egypt
item.description: null On Aug. 2, 2027, I'll be in Luxor, Egypt, to witness what could be the greatest total solar eclipse of my life. I've seen nine total solar eclipses across the world, but this one promises to be different. For a remarkable six minutes and 22 seconds, the moon will completely cover the sun, plunging Egypt's ancient temples and monuments into eerie twilight as the solar corona bursts into view. I've been calling it the "eclipse of the century" for many years, and for good reason. It will be the longest total solar eclipse until 2114 — and the longest on land of the 21st century — and it will take place in one of the most extraordinary places on Earth. What could go wrong? I've chased eclipses long enough to know that the celestial mechanics are the easy part. The moon will arrive exactly on schedule — that's guaranteed. Everything else — the weather, the crowds, the transport, the equipment and the people — is rather less predictable. From the possibility of dust storms to uncertainty about whether boats will even be allowed to move on the Nile, there are plenty of reasons to be slightly wary about what awaits eclipse chasers after the ultimate bragging rights on Aug. 2, 2027. Here are the 10 things worrying me most about the 2027 total solar eclipse in Egypt. A dust storm could make the eclipsed sun less impressive. (Image credit: Grant Faint via Getty Images) 1. A sudden dust storm The chances of cloud-free skies in Luxor and anywhere in Upper Egypt in August are exceptionally high — close to 100%. That's almost unheard of in eclipse-chasing. However, clouds aren't the only thing that can obscure the sun. Dust and sand are potential hazards in the Egyptian desert, and a dust storm at the wrong moment could affect—though probably not ruin—the view. Although the sun will almost certainly be visible during the eclipse, airborne dust could hide the delicate structure of the solar corona. 2. Chaos in Luxor How many people will descend on Luxor for the eclipse? August is normally a quiet month for tourism in Luxor because of the oppressive heat. In 2027, however, the city and its surrounding urban area — population about four million — could swell as eclipse chasers, tour groups, photographers and curious visitors descend. Hotels, roads, buses and archaeological sites will all face extraordinary pressure. My biggest concern isn't necessarily the number of people watching the eclipse, but the logistical chaos it will create. Let's take Mallorca as an example for the 2026 eclipse. Authorities there had a plan for its west coast, the prime viewing region. "They were going to start closing roads from 3 p.m. on the afternoon of the eclipse," said Simon Waldram , who runs astrophotography and landscape photography workshops and who drove his tour group to the intended viewing location at 8 o'clock on the morning of the eclipse. "There were already 300 cars there, and by 11 a.m. they had shut the road." Official plans can quickly change. The banks of the
item.dc:creator: Jamie Carter
item.content:encoded: null On Aug. 2, 2027, I'll be in Luxor, Egypt, to witness what could be the greatest total solar eclipse of my life. I've seen nine total solar eclipses across the world, but this one promises to be different. For a remarkable six minutes and 22 seconds, the moon will completely cover the sun, plunging Egypt's ancient temples and monuments into eerie twilight as the solar corona bursts into view. I've been calling it the "eclipse of the century" for many years, and for good reason. It will be the longest total solar eclipse until 2114 — and the longest on land of the 21st century — and it will take place in one of the most extraordinary places on Earth. What could go wrong? I've chased eclipses long enough to know that the celestial mechanics are the easy part. The moon will arrive exactly on schedule — that's guaranteed. Everything else — the weather, the crowds, the transport, the equipment and the people — is rather less predictable. From the possibility of dust storms to uncertainty about whether boats will even be allowed to move on the Nile, there are plenty of reasons to be slightly wary about what awaits eclipse chasers after the ultimate bragging rights on Aug. 2, 2027. Here are the 10 things worrying me most about the 2027 total solar eclipse in Egypt. A dust storm could make the eclipsed sun less impressive. (Image credit: Grant Faint via Getty Images) 1. A sudden dust storm The chances of cloud-free skies in Luxor and anywhere in Upper Egypt in August are exceptionally high — close to 100%. That's almost unheard of in eclipse-chasing. However, clouds aren't the only thing that can obscure the sun. Dust and sand are potential hazards in the Egyptian desert, and a dust storm at the wrong moment could affect—though probably not ruin—the view. Although the sun will almost certainly be visible during the eclipse, airborne dust could hide the delicate structure of the solar corona. 2. Chaos in Luxor How many people will descend on Luxor for the eclipse? August is normally a quiet month for tourism in Luxor because of the oppressive heat. In 2027, however, the city and its surrounding urban area — population about four million — could swell as eclipse chasers, tour groups, photographers and curious visitors descend. Hotels, roads, buses and archaeological sites will all face extraordinary pressure. My biggest concern isn't necessarily the number of people watching the eclipse, but the logistical chaos it will create. Let's take Mallorca as an example for the 2026 eclipse. Authorities there had a plan for its west coast, the prime viewing region. "They were going to start closing roads from 3 p.m. on the afternoon of the eclipse," said Simon Waldram , who runs astrophotography and landscape photography workshops and who drove his tour group to the intended viewing location at 8 o'clock on the morning of the eclipse. "There were already 300 cars there, and by 11 a.m. they had shut the road." Official plans can quickly change. The banks of the Nile at Luxor, Egypt. (Image credit: Glowimages via Getty Images) 3. Extreme heat Luxor in August is brutally hot. Temperatures can exceed 104 degrees Fahrenheit (40 degrees Celsius). Totality will strike at 1:02 p.m. local time (EEST). During the eclipse, from 11:40 a.m. to 2:26 p.m., the sun will be almost directly overhead. Many tour groups will stay on their hotel grounds or remain on cruise ships — relatively close to shade and air-con — though I'm also planning to keep a wet towel around my neck and carry plenty of water. However, the heat will affect the entire trip. "We're planning our visits in the early mornings and in the late afternoon, with midday just quiet time," said Khaled ElSamman, an Egyptologist at Nord Nile whose tour will witness the eclipse from a traditional dahabiya, a two-masted river boat, in Luxor. "There are reminders to drink water and keep hydrated, but it's easy to forget if you're not used to the environment and this much humidity loss." 4. Restrictions on the Nile I'll be traveling on the Nile, which sounds like a wonderfully romantic way to experience an eclipse. However, there's speculation that river traffic could be restricted, perhaps even from the previous day. "There might be a restriction on navigation on the Nile during the eclipse, so it's a bit hard to plan where we are going to watch it," said ElSamman. "We might end up in harbor, and maybe we won't be allowed to be in the middle of the water." The Nile will be very busy on Aug. 2, 2027. (Image credit: Ulrich Hollmann via Getty Images) 5. The enormous number of boats Even if we're safely moored in Luxor, how many other vessels will be there? The Nile looks set to be packed with cruise ships, traditional dahabiyas and smaller boats, all carrying people hoping to witness the same extraordinary event. I wonder what totality will actually look and sound like. Will there be music? Shouting? Bright lights from neighboring boats? Probably — though perhaps that's no bad thing. It's fun to experience totality in all kinds of different environments. One of my most vivid memories of the 1999 total solar eclipse in the U.K. is the atmosphere created by the people around me and the lights that came on in boats in Falmouth harbor. Perhaps the noise and excitement will become part of the magic. I just hope nobody leaves their floodlights on. 6. Camera equipment Whether eclipse chasers can bring specialist camera equipment into the country is vexing many. After all, "professional-looking" camera equipment is usually difficult to get through customs. While phones and compact cameras are fine, customs and security personnel classify large mirrorless/DSLR cameras, long telephoto lenses and heavy tripods as "professional filming gear." My reporting suggests customs officials may take a more relaxed approach to specialist camera equipment during the eclipse. However, no special customs arrangements for eclipse visitors have been confirmed. Drones are a different matter — Egypt has strict restrictions on importing and operating them, with authorization required. Bringing a drone to see this eclipse would be a mistake. 7. Keeping a camera cool Will cameras struggle in the extreme heat? (Image credit: fhm via Getty Images) Photographing a total solar eclipse involves pointing equipment towards the sun for an extended period, using appropriate solar filters during the partial phases. In Luxor's extreme August temperatures — and with the sun almost directly overhead — overheating could become a serious issue, particularly for cameras recording video or running continuously. Eclipse chasers will need to keep equipment shaded and as cool as possible. I'll just hope to have my trusty image-stabilized binoculars with me. I bought them a decade ago specifically for total solar eclipses, and they've given me some of the most extraordinary views and moments of my life. 8. Overcrowded temples Watching a total solar eclipse from Karnak or another ancient Egyptian temple sounds almost impossibly romantic. But the reality could be very different. Popular archaeological sites, such as Karnak, Luxor Temple, Hatshepsut and the Valley of the Kings, could be overwhelmed by visitors. That could mean crowded entrances, long queues and limited facilities. Besides, with the eclipsed sun close to the zenith, those spectacular images of totality framed between ancient columns may be more fantasy than reality. It may be wise to avoid the crowds — and with myriad temples and ruins near Luxor, that's likely possible. "You want to make sure you're not fighting with 10,000 other tourists trying to see the same thing," said Waldram. Queueing for hours at Karnak is not the best way to enjoy one of nature's greatest events. Entrance to Ramses III temple, Karnak, in Luxor, Egypt. (Image credit: Sergio Pitamitz/robertharding via Getty Images) 9. Eclipse-gouging Every eclipse chaser who plans and books a hotel years in advance dreads the email that often ar

item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 21, 1676: Danish astronomer discovers speed of light — by accident — while observing Jupiter's moon Io
item.description: null On Nov. 21, 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer discovered the speed of light . Before Rømer figured it out, scientists thought that light travels instantaneously, or infinitely fast. Rømer disproved this almost by accident when he was studying Jupiter's moon Io . He was trying to figure out how long it takes Io to orbit Jupiter in hopes of using it as a cosmic clock. He watched Io disappear behind Jupiter and reappear on the other side. He did this over and over every 42 hours for years. To his surprise, the timing of the eclipses was not consistent. When Earth was closest to Jupiter, the eclipses happened 11 minutes early. Likewise, when the two planets were farthest away, the eclipses were 11 minutes behind schedule. Rømer figured out the pattern and made an accurate prediction for Io's eclipse on Nov. 9, 1676. Then on Nov. 21, he took his findings to the Royal Academy of Sciences and explained that a finite speed of light must be responsible. Danish astronomer Ole Rømer (Image credit: Wikimedia Commons) Why it mattered Understanding that the speed of light is a constant is the key that opened our ability to gauge the scale of the universe, as well as was central to developing modern physics. "The speed of light becomes a sort of ultimate speed limit," Live Science explained in an article about why the speed of light matters. "In fact, objects with mass, be they cars or neutrinos, can't reach the speed of light because they would need infinite energy to do so."

item.title: This Week In Space podcast: Episode 237 — A Fond Farewell
item.description: null On Episode 237 of This Week In Space , Tariq Malik and Rod Pyle sign off — temporarily — with a look at space news, a bushel of space jokes, and a recap of some of our funniest moments. Welcome to the last episode of This Week in Space . It's been a good run — including our betas, we produced about 240 episodes of the show, and had a blast doing it. We appreciate all of you, our fine listeners, for accompanying us on this journey, and are working to continue in a new venue in early 2027. To track our progress, and get your weekly fix of Rod's terrible space humor, find us on Instagram and Facebook: @rodandtariq Download or subscribe to this show at: https://twit.tv/shows/this-week-in-space . Get episodes ad-free with Club TWiT at https://twit.tv/clubtwit Space news of the week Sir Brian May adds new dimension to Hera asteroid Russian Military Satellite’s Approach to American Spacecraft Looked Like a Weapons Operation, US Says Google Selects Blue Origin’s New Glenn for Project Suncatcher Voyager 1 team, unbowed by communications glitch, celebrates epic 1-light-day distance milestone Pakistani astronaut set to become 1st international visitor to China's Tiangong space station this month Model Falcon 9! TOP TELESCOPE PICK: (Image credit: Celestron) Looking for a telescope to see planets and comets? We recommend the Celestron Astro Fi 102 as the top pick in our best beginner's telescope guide . Finally, did you know you can launch your own SpaceX rocket? Model rocket maker Estes' stunning scale model of a Falcon 9 rocket that you can pick up now. The launchable model is a detailed recreation of the Falcon 9 and retails for $149.99. You can save 10% by using the code IN-COLLECTSPACE at checkout , courtesy of our partners collectSPACE.com. About This Week In Space This Week in Space covers the new space age. Every Friday we take a deep dive into a fascinating topic. What's happening with the new race to the moon and other planets? When will SpaceX really send people to Mars? Join Rod Pyle and Tariq Malik from Space.com as they tackle those questions and more each week on Friday afternoons. You can subscribe today on your favorite podcatcher.

item.title: 'Star Trek: First Contact' at 30: Resistance is futile when it comes to the 'Next Generation' crew's greatest big-screen adventure
item.description:
Richard's love affair with outer space started when he saw the original "Star Wars" on TV aged four, and he spent much of the ’90s watching "Star Trek”, "Babylon 5” and “The X-Files" with his mum. After studying physics at university, he became a journalist, swapped science fact for science fiction, and hit the jackpot when he joined the team at SFX, the UK's biggest sci-fi and fantasy magazine. He liked it so much he stayed there for 12 years, four of them as editor. 

He's since gone freelance and passes his time writing about "Star Wars", "Star Trek" and superheroes for the likes of SFX, Total Film, TechRadar and GamesRadar+. He has met five Doctors, two Starfleet captains and one Luke Skywalker, and once sat in the cockpit of "Red Dwarf"'s Starbug.  

Following the sad news of Sir Patrick Stewart's passing , there's been no shortage of discussion about his best moments as Captain Jean-Luc Picard . "The Inner Light"'s life in 25 minutes is a strong contender, as are the courtroom grandstanding in "The Measure of a Man" and his insistence (under extreme torture) that "there are four lights!" in "Chain of Command". But for this writer's money, it's hard to look past a nine-minute sequence in "Star Trek: First Contact", which turns 30 this weekend. With the Borg overrunning the newly launched USS Enterprise-E, Picard — who has long-standing beef with the Collective, following his assimilation in classic "The Next Generation" story " The Best of Both Worlds " — orders his crew to fight the cybernetic nasties hand-to-hand if required, defying their pleas to activate the ship's self-destruct system and retreat. He even calls Worf — not a man renowned for dodging a fight — a coward, prompting the Klingon to respond that, "If you were any other man, I would kill you where you stand." Ouch. But following some impassioned talk about making the Borg "pay for what they've done", he's finally talked down from his rage by 21st-century stowaway Lily Sloane (Alfre Woodard). She points out that his Moby-Dick-esque obsession is on the verge of going full Ahab, and he eventually sees sense, issuing the order to abandon the Enterprise and destroy the hive. It's a masterclass showcasing the ever-brilliant Stewart's impressive range, as the out-of-control captain's rarely seen temper reaches fever pitch, before normal service is resumed. His subsequent apology to Worf — "As a matter of fact, I think you're the bravest man I've ever known" — is simply perfect. And just as the franchise's zenith, "The Wrath of Khan", is built around Kirk and Khan's decades-old feud, "First Contact" is precision engineered to get the most out of Jean-Luc. This was the right "Star Trek" at the right time, a film that put "TNG"'s greatest villains on a collision course with the origins of Starfleet. item.content:encoded:
Richard's love affair with outer space started when he saw the original "Star Wars" on TV aged four, and he spent much of the ’90s watching "Star Trek”, "Babylon 5” and “The X-Files" with his mum. He liked it so much he stayed there for 12 years, four of them as editor. 

He's since gone freelance and passes his time writing about "Star Wars", "Star Trek" and superheroes for the likes of SFX, Total Film, TechRadar and GamesRadar+. He has met five Doctors, two Starfleet captains and one Luke Skywalker, and once sat in the cockpit of "Red Dwarf"'s Starbug.  

Following the sad news of Sir Patrick Stewart's passing , there's been no shortage of discussion about his best moments as Captain Jean-Luc Picard . "The Inner Light"'s life in 25 minutes is a strong contender, as are the courtroom grandstanding in "The Measure of a Man" and his insistence (under extreme torture) that "there are four lights!" in "Chain of Command". But for this writer's money, it's hard to look past a nine-minute sequence in "Star Trek: First Contact", which turns 30 this weekend. With the Borg overrunning the newly launched USS Enterprise-E, Picard — who has long-standing beef with the Collective, following his assimilation in classic "The Next Generation" story " The Best of Both Worlds " — orders his crew to fight the cybernetic nasties hand-to-hand if required, defying their pleas to activate the ship's self-destruct system and retreat. He even calls Worf — not a man renowned for dodging a fight — a coward, prompting the Klingon to respond that, "If you were any other man, I would kill you where you stand." Ouch. But following some impassioned talk about making the Borg "pay for what they've done", he's finally talked down from his rage by 21st-century stowaway Lily Sloane (Alfre Woodard). She points out that his Moby-Dick-esque obsession is on the verge of going full Ahab, and he eventually sees sense, issuing the order to abandon the Enterprise and destroy the hive. It's a masterclass showcasing the ever-brilliant Stewart's impressive range, as the out-of-control captain's rarely seen temper reaches fever pitch, before normal service is resumed. His subsequent apology to Worf — "As a matter of fact, I think you're the bravest man I've ever known" — is simply perfect. And just as the franchise's zenith, "The Wrath of Khan", is built around Kirk and Khan's decades-old feud, "First Contact" is precision engineered to get the most out of Jean-Luc. This was the right "Star Trek" at the right time, a film that put "TNG"'s greatest villains on a collision course with the origins of Starfleet. It's not quite "Khan", of course — what is? — but it deserves to be mentioned in the same breath. (Image credit: Paramount) In 1996, the "odd numbers bad, even numbers good" rule of "Trek" films still, more or less, rang true. 1994's "Generations", rushed out a few months after " The Next Generation " ended its seven-year run on TV, had done decent business, but the seventh movie's convoluted "passing the baton" storyline had left many fans cold. Now, however, with Kirk killed off, it was time for Picard and his crew to explore the big-screen frontier alone. William Shatner actually pitched a resurrection storyline for Kirk, but "Trek" executive producer/overlord Rick Berman ruled that it was a little too soon to bring the good captain back. Instead, he hired "Generations" scripters and "TNG"/"Deep Space Nine" writers' room regulars Brannon Braga and Ronald D. Moore to craft an eighth movie capable of living up to its even-numbered predecessors. While "Generations" had been written to an extremely restrictive brief, Braga and Moore were given much more freedom the second time out. Berman was keen on a time-travel storyline while Braga lobbied for the fan-favorite Borg, and early on they explored the idea of taking the Collective back to Renaissance Italy. These plans were abandoned when Stewart vetoed the idea of wearing tights. (Image credit: Paramount) They eventually zeroed in on April 5, 2063 , the date Zefram Cochrane (a character who'd previously appeared in Original Series episode "Metamorphosis") made humanity's first warp flight and put Earth on the radar of a passing Vulcan ship. "We landed on the idea of what I called the 'Star Trek' nativity scene — the birth of 'Star Trek'," Braga said in "The Fifty-Year Mission" by Mark A Altman and Edward Gross. "The three wise Vulcans who arrive on Earth and step out of their ship for our first contact with an extraterrestrial species. And the Borg were going to prevent that from happening, which really struck a bullseye for me, because it would allow non-'Star Trek' people to understand why 'Star Trek' matters by putting the crew and the Borg back in that time frame. I thought it would appeal to a larger audience. 'Star Trek' itself was at stake, and that was super cool to me." (Image credit: Paramount) Paramount reportedly flirted with big-name directors like Ridley Scott (" Alien ", " Blade Runner ") and John McTiernan ("Predator", "Die Hard"), before settling on Jonathan Frakes. Although this would be Frakes' first movie, the man best known for playing Commander Riker had directed numerous "Trek" episodes. Berman believed that an understanding of the franchise's DNA was more important than big-screen experience. The film wastes little time on exposition for "Trek" newbies, with just a short dream sequence to explain away Picard's history with the Borg. With a single Borg Cube on course for Earth, the Federation fleet mobilizes to fight them off. They're getting their asses well and truly kicked, too, until the Enterprise warps into the battle. The Cube is ultimately destroyed but still manages to dispatch a Sphere, which uses chronometric particles to travel back to 2063 in order to assimilate Earth in the past. Picard has no choice but to follow them back to "repair whatever damage they've done". (Image credit: Paramount) They arrive in a post-World War III Montana, where Cochrane has constructed his prototype faster-than-light vessel, the Phoenix. Played by "Babe" star James Cromwell (who'd already guest-starred in a trio of "TNG" episodes), Cochrane is some way from the man future history has remembered: a hard-drinking womanizer more motivated by potential riches than the betterment of mankind. A man uncomfortable with the idea that a high school will one day bear his name. But as some of the crew work to repair the damage caused by the Sphere's bombing raid, there are bigger problems in orbit. Borg survivors have beamed on board the Enterprise and started assimilating the vessel and its crew. Initial drafts of the script saw Riker leading the ship-based resistance while Picard remained on Earth, but — at Stewart's request — Braga and Moore flipped things round to bring the captain face-to-face with his nemesis. It proved to be a really smart move, as Stewart got to ditch his new-look Starfleet uniform and run around the Enterprise as a full-on action hero in a John McClane-style vest. (Image credit: Paramount) These Borg had been given a multiplex upgrade, with massively improved prosthetics and new extendable tendrils that injected nanoprobes to assimilate a victim from within. Frakes played up the horror aspects of the Collective, portraying them as a horde of mindless cybernetic zombies, while using "Alien" and " Aliens " as inspiration. "[Ridley Scott and James Cameron] made it clear that when it comes to villains, the more that's suggested, the scarier they are," Frakes explained. "I tried to get that with the Borg." The biggest change came at the head of the organization, where — at the suggestion of Paramount executive Jonathan Dolgen — "First Contact" introduced a previously unseen

item.title: SpaceX will retire 1st Starship upper stage ever caught by 'chopsticks,' Elon Musk says
item.description: null The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again. That vehicle, known as Ship 42, launched Nov. 13 on Starship 's 15th test flight. A day later, it returned from orbit, nestling softly into the "chopstick" arms of its launch tower at SpaceX 's Starbase site in South Texas. Ship 42 made it through Flight 15 in good condition, according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk , who said it "could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment." But that's not going to happen. "In this case, because it's kind of an historic ship, we're going to, I think, not take any chances with the ship and just kind of leave it for public display, because what it's done is historic," Musk said on Wednesday (Nov. 18) during a discussion at the TomorrowX Summit . He didn't say where Ship would be put on display, but the likeliest locale is Starbase, SpaceX's Starship manufacturing and launch hub. (SpaceX plans to shift most Starship launches to its new Starbase Louisiana site, but construction has yet to begin on that $100 billion complex.) Musk participated virtually in the TomorrowX conversation, which was moderated by two friends of his, the venture capitalists Gavin Baker and Antonio Gracias. (TomorrowX took place in Austin, Texas, but Musk was in China on Wednesday as part of President Trump's delegation for his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.) The world's richest man expounded on Ship 42's historic achievement, explaining that it gets SpaceX much closer to the "holy grail of rocketry" — a fully and rapidly reusable launch vehicle. Before Flight 15, SpaceX had already caught Starship's first-stage booster, known as Super Heavy, on three separate occasions , and it had reflown a booster twice. But the company had never attempted a Ship catch, which is a taller order, given how much faster and farther Starship upper stages fly. So snagging Ship on the first try was a very big deal, according to Musk. "Everyone knew, within SpaceX, at least, how important this milestone was, and that it was really something fundamental and profound — that Starship will be the first-ever fully reusable orbital space system," he told Baker and Gracias on Wednesday. The Ship upper stage of SpaceX's Starship megarocket comes back to its launch tower for a "chopsticks" catch on Nov. 14, 2026, during the vehicle's 15th test flight. (Image credit: SpaceX) And SpaceX is very serious about Starship reuse. Musk has said that the company wants to launch about 10,000 Starship missions per year by 2030. This mind-boggling cadence will help the company build out two enormous megaconstellations in low Earth orbit — the next iteration of its Starlink broadband network, which will consist of about 100,000 satellites , and its Starmind AI data-center constellation, which will be 10 times bigger than that . Assembly of that new Starlink network is already underway. Ship carried 26 of the next-gen internet spacecraft up for the first time on F

item.title: European-Japanese BepiColombo mission becomes 2nd ever to arrive in orbit around Mercury
item.description: null Update for 2:50 p.m. ET on Nov. 23: On Sunday afternoon (Nov. 22), the BepiColombo team announced that, while the spacecraft did successfully arrive in orbit around Mercury on Saturday (Nov. 21), the engine burn that got it there was cut short due to a software glitch. On Monday (Nov. 23), we got another update : BepiColombo "is safe and in a stable orbit around Mercury" and is on track for the next big milestone: The separation of its two orbiters on Dec. 9. For just the second time ever, Mercury has received a robotic visitor from Earth. The BepiColombo mission — a joint effort of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency ( JAXA ) — arrived in orbit around Mercury on Saturday (Nov. 21), more than eight years after leaving its home planet. Before BepiColombo, just one spacecraft had ever circled the solar system's innermost planet: NASA's MESSENGER , which did so from March 2011 to April 2015. BepiColombo consists of two main spacecraft: ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO), also known as Mio. The duo launched — along with a power and propulsion element called the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) — aboard an Ariane 5 rocket from French Guiana in October 2018 , beginning a long and looping trip through the inner solar system. Mercury is a difficult planet to reach because it's so close to the sun . Spacecraft approaching the planet are accelerated to high velocities by the immense gravitational pull of our star and must therefore shed a great deal of kinetic energy to be captured by Mercury's much weaker tug. So the BepiColombo team designed a trajectory that featured one flyby of Earth , two of Venus and six of Mercury over the course of about seven years. That flight time was increased by a year , however, after the mission suffered an issue with its solar panels, which reduced the power available for the MTM's electric thrusters. BepiColombo's arrival at Mercury will take a total of about six months. (Image credit: European Space Agency) Saturday's orbital insertion came after a 37-minute-long engine burn, which began at 1:24 p.m. EST (1824 GMT). There was a bit drama involved, however, as confirmation of the maneuver's success didn't come for several hours afterward. "We've heard back from Bepi — the spacecraft is now in contact with the ground and the teams at ESOC [the European Space Operations Centre] are busy assessing the telemetry. Flight Dynamics already has confirmed it achieved orbital capture around Mercury! Early next week we'll share the next update with the upcoming steps," the mission team said via X on Saturday evening. We've heard back from Bepi - the spacecraft is now in contact with the ground and the teams at ESOC are busy assessing the telemetry. So the BepiColombo team designed a trajectory that featured one flyby of Earth , two of Venus and six of Mercury over the course of about seven years. That flight time was increased by a year , however, after the mission suffered an issue with its solar panels, which reduced the power available for the MTM's electric thrusters. BepiColombo's arrival at Mercury will take a total of about six months. (Image credit: European Space Agency) Saturday's orbital insertion came after a 37-minute-long engine burn, which began at 1:24 p.m. EST (1824 GMT). There was a bit drama involved, however, as confirmation of the maneuver's success didn't come for several hours afterward. "We've heard back from Bepi — the spacecraft is now in contact with the ground and the teams at ESOC [the European Space Operations Centre] are busy assessing the telemetry. Flight Dynamics already has confirmed it achieved orbital capture around Mercury! Early next week we'll share the next update with the upcoming steps," the mission team said via X on Saturday evening. We've heard back from Bepi - the spacecraft is now in contact with the ground and the teams at ESOC are busy assessing the telemetry. Flight Dynamics already has confirmed it achieved orbital capture around Mercury!Early next week we'll share the next update with the upcoming steps. November 22, 2026 Orbital insertion is the latest milestone in BepiColombo's Mercury arrival phase, which is expected to take about six months in total. Arrival began on Sept. 3, when the MTM released MPO and Mio. The two orbiters remain connected today; they won't separate until Dec. 9 or thereabouts. Shortly thereafter, Mio will settle into its final orbit, a highly elliptical path that will take it over Mercury's poles. MPO is also destined for a polar orbit, though a much less elliptical one than Mio's; the ESA probe will conduct a series of engine burns before finally getting there on March 10, 2027. BepiColombo — which is named after the late Italian scientist and mathematician Giuseppe "Bepi" Colombo — won't start doing science work until April 6, 2027. The two probes will gather complementary data from their different vantage points, shedding a great deal of light on a mysterious world. "The mission will study all aspects of Mercury, from the structure and dynamics of its magnetosphere and how it interacts with the solar wind , to its internal structure with its large iron core, and the origin of the planet’s magnetic field," ESA officials wrote in a BepiColombo mission description . "The data will enable scientists to understand more about the origin and evolution of a planet located close to its parent star, and a better understanding of the overall evolution of our solar system," they added. Editor's note: This story was updated at 11:15 a.m. ET on Nov. 22 with news off successful orbital arrival.

item.title: SpaceX launches classified mission for US Space Force from California (video)
item.description: null SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force tonight (Nov. 20), sending a mystery payload to orbit from California's central coast. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:20 p.m. EST (8:20 p.m. local California time; 0420 GMT on Nov. 21), on a Space Force mission called USSF-317. The Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth about 8.5 minutes later, touching down in the Pacific Ocean atop the SpaceX drone ship "Of Course I Still Love You." It was the 11th launch and landing for this booster, which is designated B1100. A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launches the USSF-317 mission for the U.S. Space Force from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California on Nov. 20, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) SpaceX ended its launch webcast just after that touchdown, so we didn't get to see the Falcon 9's upper stage power its way to orbit. USSF-317 is a classified mission, so we don't know what the upper stage is carrying or where exactly it's headed. However, some experts think that USSF-317 may be hauling a batch of SpaceX's Starshield satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO) for the Space Force's Space Based Sensing and Targeting portfolio, which helps the military keep tabs on potential targets around the world. The Falcon 9's first stage rests on the deck of a drone ship after launching the USSF-317 mission. (Image credit: SpaceX) Previous Booster 1100 missions NROL-105 | USSF-385 | 8 Starlink missions USSF-317 was the 121st Falcon 9 launch of 2026 and the third mission that SpaceX has launched for the Space Force so far in November. The vast majority of this year's Falcon 9 missions — about 70% of them — have been devoted to building out SpaceX's Starlink LEO internet constellation, which currently consists of more than 11,000 satellites. The Falcon 9 has been putting up incredible numbers lately — it flew a whopping 165 times in 2025 , for example — but the workhorse rocket is on its way out . SpaceX plans to retire both it and the Falcon Heavy in favor of its fully reusable Starship megarocket, which deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites on its most recent two test flights .

item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 20, 1998: Russia launches 1st module of International Space Station as construction begins on the largest human-built structure in orbit
item.description: null On Nov. 20, 1998, the first piece of the International Space Station launched into orbit. The 42,000-pound module is called Zarya, and it's about the size of a tour bus. Zarya launched on board a Russian Proton rocket . Two weeks later, NASA's STS-88 shuttle mission aboard Endeavour brought the Unity module into space. The STS-88 astronauts connected the two modules in orbit. Zarya was built by the Russians, but it was paid for by the United States. NASA contracted a Russian company to build it for half the price of what the American company Lockheed Martin would have charged. These days, Zarya is mainly used for storage and for external fuel tanks. The module also has docking ports for Russian Progress cargo ships and Soyuz spacecraft that carry crews to and from the space station. Today, the I nternational Space Station is about the size of a football field and typically hosts up to seven crewmembers. But back in 1998, it was a pretty tight squeeze. A Russian Proton rocket launches the core Zarya module of the International Space Station (left), which can be seen in orbit (right) during the first mission to the station in 1998. (Image credit: NASA/Roscosmos) Why it mattered As of this writing, the International Space Station is 28 years old, and has seen steady rotating crews of astronauts since the year 2000 (for 26 years and counting). It is a marvel of space engineering, but every engineering marvel begins the same: with the first piece. And that is what the Zarya module is: The foundation of the International Space Station. Zarya, also known as the Functional Cargo Block (or Russian acronym FGB), is the core module of the space station around which every other module was attached. It weighed 42,600 pounds at launch and is just aver 41 feet long and 13.5 feet wide. Inside, it boasts a total habitable volume of 1,650 cubic feet. The Zarya and Unity modules are connecting in orbit to build the International Space Station. NASA The Zarya and Unity modules are connecting in orbit to build the International Space Station. NASA The Zarya and Unity modules are connecting in orbit to build the International Space Station. NASA NASA paid $220 million for Zarya's construction at the Krunichev State Research and Production Space Center in Moscow, with work beginning in 1994 and ending in 1998. The module is a central hub based on the success of Russia's Salyut space station designs , with two solar arrays for power and 16 external tanks to store propellant. Today, the I nternational Space Station is about the size of a football field and typically hosts up to seven crewmembers. But back in 1998, it was a pretty tight squeeze. A Russian Proton rocket launches the core Zarya module of the International Space Station (left), which can be seen in orbit (right) during the first mission to the station in 1998. (Image credit: NASA/Roscosmos) Why it mattered As of this writing, the International Space Station is 28 years old, and has seen steady rotating crews of astronauts since the year 2000 (for 26 years and counting). It is a marvel of space engineering, but every engineering marvel begins the same: with the first piece. And that is what the Zarya module is: The foundation of the International Space Station. It weighed 42,600 pounds at launch and is just aver 41 feet long and 13.5 feet wide. Inside, it boasts a total habitable volume of 1,650 cubic feet. The Zarya and Unity modules are connecting in orbit to build the International Space Station. NASA The Zarya and Unity modules are connecting in orbit to build the International Space Station. NASA The Zarya and Unity modules are connecting in orbit to build the International Space Station. NASA NASA paid $220 million for Zarya's construction at the Krunichev State Research and Production Space Center in Moscow, with work beginning in 1994 and ending in 1998. The module is a central hub based on the success of Russia's Salyut space station designs , with two solar arrays for power and 16 external tanks to store propellant. While NASA's space shuttle Endeavour was the first to meet Zarya (and attach NASA's core Unity connecting module to it), it wasn't until Russia'z Zvezda service launched in 2000 and docked with Zarya's aft that the fledgling space station was large enough to accomodate its first three-person crew, Expedition 1. Over the last 28 years, giant backbone-like metal trusses, solar wings and many other modules (built by Russia, NASA, Europe, Canada and Japan) have greatly expanded the living area of the station. Many ISS components could not be tested with one another on the ground, meaning the first time they were attached was in space during construction. The result is a feat of space construction that has only recently seen a rival as China works to expand its own Tiangong space station . Want more space history? item.title: Don't turn the moon into the Wild West, scientists warn
item.description:
Tereza is a London-based science and technology journalist, aspiring fiction writer and amateur gymnast. Originally from Prague, the Czech Republic, she spent the first seven years of her career working as a reporter, script-writer and presenter for various TV programmes of the Czech Public Service Television. She later took a career break to pursue further education and added a Master's in Science from the International Space University, France, to her Bachelor's in Journalism and Master's in Cultural Anthropology from Prague's Charles University. She worked as a reporter at the Engineering and Technology magazine, freelanced for a range of publications including Live Science, Space.com, Professional Engineering, Via Satellite and Space News and served as a maternity cover science editor at the European Space Agency.

Researchers are calling for a moratorium on industrial exploitation of the moon, fearing that rapid development could cause irreversible environmental damage and destroy invaluable scientific material. Both China and the U.S. are pushing forward with plans to establish permanent human settlements on the moon by the end of the next decade. Commercial players want to build businesses supporting these future explorers by mining for resources such as water , construction materials, industrial metals and rare earth minerals. However, some scientists argue that a temporary ban on lunar industrialization is necessary to allow regulations to catch up and limit what can be allowed in order to prevent a moon rush from destroying the pristine lunar environment. Two such researchers are Florian Rabitz, a professor of climate and technology governance at Vilnius University in Lithuania, and Xiao-Shan Yap, an assistant professor of Earth-space sustainability at Utrecht University in the Netherlands. In a piece published last month in the journal Global Environmental Politics , the pair call for "robust international regulations" and "broad and inclusive deliberation" to allow the global community to carefully consider the impact of economic activities on the moon. In addition to the threat to the scientifically priceless lunar landscape, the researchers also object to the colonization of the moon by a small number of powerful players — namely China, the U.S. and their respective close allies. "With the moon it's absolutely clear that whoever is doing the big infrastructure work is going to be asserting their position, including by defining their own exclusive territories," Rabitz said in a statement . "That shouldn't be the Wild West." Rabitz pointed out that, although the United Nations' 1967 Outer Space Treaty prevents individual nations from appropriating the moon, Earth's natural satellite and its valuable resources are unlikely to remain truly neutral territory if its exploitation is going to be led by a small number of powerful nations.

item.title: ‘The greatest game ever made’: readers and Guardian staff on Grand Theft Auto VI
item.description: Rockstar’s newest installment of its hit franchise still has plenty of action, along with a dose of ‘healthy masculinity’ Described as the biggest entertainment launch in history, the new Grand Theft Auto game has prompted avid fans around the world to take the day off work, stock up on snacks and celebrate its arrival after 13 years of waiting. While some have already spent hours immersed in the game’s criminal escapades, others have found themselves doing household chores, building houses or simply taking in the scenery – which includes more than 170 flora and fauna species native to Florida . GTA VI has generated extraordinary global anticipation for its action-packed gameplay, but players are now finding new delight in the game’s more intimate moments. Continue reading...

item.title: Asali Africa: Serves Up ‘There’s Rice at Home’ A New Cooking Series Hosted by Chef Soliat Bada
item.description: Chef Soliat Bada Anyone who grew up in a Nigerian home knows the line. You suggest buying food outside, and before you finish the sentence, someone reminds you that there’s rice at home. It is usually the end of the conversation. In Asali Africa’s new series, it is where the conversation starts. There’s Rice at Home is a cooking and conversation show from Asali Africa, the Lagos-based creative development agency, hosted by Chef Soliat Bada . In each episode, Soliat cooks one rice dish with a guest, and while the pot does its work, the two get into the kind of talk that usually happens around food: family, money and what success really looks like. Rice is the most ordinary thing in a Nigerian kitchen, and the show makes a good case that it doesn’t have to taste ordinary. Over five episodes, released every two weeks, the menu travels from Jamaica to Saudi Arabia, back home to Nigeria and on to Louisiana. You don’t just watch the food get made, either. The recipes are written up in full on Asali Africa’s website, with the ingredients and method laid out step by step, so you can watch Soliat cook a dish and then make it in your own kitchen. The season opens with Rice and Peas with Oxtail, the Jamaican Sunday staple of rice cooked in coconut milk with red kidney beans (the “peas”), served beside rich, slow-cooked oxtail. Soliat’s guest is Michael Famoroti , co-founder of Stears, and their conversation turns to family and black tax: the expectation that once you start earning, you start supporting the people who raised you. Read the full recipe for Rice and Peas with Oxtail . Rice and peas with oxtail, from Episode 1 Soliat Bada and Michael Famoroti in Episode 1 Episode 2 moves to the Gulf for lamb kabsa, Saudi Arabia’s national dish, fragrant with dried lime and seven spice. Soliat is joined by Bella Adeleke , CEO of Asali Africa and founder of the fashion label Garbe, for a conversation about redefining success. Read the full recipe for Lamb Kabsa . Lamb kabsa, from Episode 2 Still to come are Nigerian fried rice with fried turkey and dodo, cooked with Toyin Jolapamo and Nneoma Mere; jambalaya with Goldie Iyamu and Vanessa Iloenyosi ; and a season finale with Edwin Okolo and Temi Omolehinwa. For more on Asali Africa and the products and ideas it develops, visit asali.africa . Episodes 1 and 2 are out now on YouTube. Watch Episode 1 below. https://www.youtube.com/embed/-6Ux0-vNDnw Sponsored Content The post Asali Africa: Serves Up ‘There’s Rice at Home’ A New Cooking Series Hosted by Chef Soliat Bada appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Beyond the Mini LED Label: What Should Define Good Mini LED Performance?
item.description: The presence of Mini LED tells a shopper something important about the light source behind an LCD panel. It does not, by itself, explain how that light is arranged, divided or controlled. Those implementation choices can have a major influence on contrast, black level performance, highlight control and the visibility of blooming in difficult scenes. From Presence To Performance That distinction matters because a category becomes more useful to consumers when it can be evaluated through clear performance principles rather than through a technology name alone. For Mini LED, three factors provide a practical starting point. The first is hardware local dimming. In a hardware based system, physical groups of LEDs can be brightened, dimmed or switched off independently across different areas of the screen. This gives the television more direct control over how light is distributed within a single image. The second is local dimming zone count and precision. A higher number of independently controlled zones can allow the backlight to respond in smaller areas, which can improve separation between bright highlights and surrounding dark regions when other major conditions are comparable. The number itself is not the whole story, but it is a useful indicator of how granular the backlight system can be. The third is backlight architecture. Full Array Local Dimming places controllable zones across the area behind the panel, providing the physical foundation for more localized light management than designs that illuminate the panel from the edges or operate the backlight more uniformly. Together, these three elements move the Mini LED conversation from a simple question of whether the technology is present to a more useful question: how effectively is the light being controlled? Where TCL Enters The Category Conversation TCL is relevant to that discussion because Mini LED has become a significant part of its global television business. According to Omdia data cited in TCL Electronics interim results, TCL ranked No. 1 globally by Mini LED TV shipment volume in the first half of 2026. TCL reported 2.43 million Mini LED TV shipments during the period, representing 77.1% year on year growth. That position follows a strong 2025, when TCL reported, based on Omdia data, a 31.1% share of global Mini LED TV shipments and 118.0% year on year shipment growth. Market scale does not, on its own, define technology leadership. What it does provide is evidence that a manufacturer has become an important participant in how the category develops. For a company operating at that scale, leadership increasingly includes helping make the technology easier to understand and giving consumers clearer ways to evaluate what they are buying. This gives the television more direct control over how light is distributed within a single image. The second is local dimming zone count and precision. A higher number of independently controlled zones can allow the backlight to respond in smaller areas, which can improve separation between bright highlights and surrounding dark regions when other major conditions are comparable. Where TCL Enters The Category Conversation TCL is relevant to that discussion because Mini LED has become a significant part of its global television business. That position follows a strong 2025, when TCL reported, based on Omdia data, a 31.1% share of global Mini LED TV shipments and 118.0% year on year shipment growth. Market scale does not, on its own, define technology leadership. What it does provide is evidence that a manufacturer has become an important participant in how the category develops. For a company operating at that scale, leadership increasingly includes helping make the technology easier to understand and giving consumers clearer ways to evaluate what they are buying. Defining Category Leadership Category leadership in Mini LED should therefore be broader than shipment rankings. It can be understood through four connected areas: sustained market scale, continued investment in the fundamentals of backlight performance, clearer performance criteria, and education that helps consumers distinguish between different implementations of the technology. This is where the idea of good Mini LED becomes useful. It does not require creating a new certification or suggesting that every television should perform identically. It simply encourages a more complete discussion of the hardware and architecture that sit behind the Mini LED name. item.title: Lagos Hosts 2026 International Theatre Festival, Featuring Local and International Productions
item.description: The third edition of the Lagos International Theatre Festival (LITF) has concluded successfully, attracting over 20,000 attendees from November 9 to 15, 2026. Featuring more than 25 productions, international performances from Kenya, Brazil, Norway and Canada, high-profile diplomatic engagements and a spectacular Opening Night Gala, the festival reinforced its growing position as an important platform for showcasing Nigerian creativity and connecting global theatre communities. The impressive turnout, diversity of productions and international participation demonstrated the growing appetite for live theatre and the potential of cultural platforms to stimulate creative enterprise, encourage international collaboration and strengthen Nigeria’s global cultural presence. A Vision For Global Recognition Speaking on the success of the festival, Founder and Creative Producer, Bolanle Austen-Peters , said: “Our ambition has always been to create more than a theatre festival. We want to build a platform that places Lagos firmly on the global cultural map, gives African stories the international visibility they deserve and creates meaningful opportunities for our artists. Welcoming over 20,000 attendees, presenting more than 25 productions and bringing international performers from four countries to Lagos is a powerful affirmation of this vision. Theatre is not just entertainment; it is an instrument of cultural identity, economic opportunity and global influence. The Stage Is Everywhere, and Africa must claim its rightful place on that stage.” A Week Of Culture And Collaboration The festival opened on November 9 with Theatre Meets Food at Kaly Restaurant, featuring celebrated chef Hilda Baci in a unique fusion of culinary artistry and live performance. The week also featured diplomatic and cultural engagements hosted by the United States Consul General in Lagos and the British Embassy, alongside a networking reception organised by the British Council for festival directors and participating production companies. These engagements highlighted the importance of international partnerships and cultural diplomacy in advancing Nigeria’s creative industry. A Celebration Of Excellence A major highlight was the Opening Night Gala, held on November 13 at Shell Hall, MUSON Centre, which welcomed over 1,000 guests, including the Governor of Lagos State, Babajide Olusola Sanwo-Olu ; the Chargé d’Affaires of the US Mission in Nigeria; the US Consul General; the British Deputy High Commissioner; the Consul General of Brazil; the Consul General of South Africa, the Ambassador of the Republic of Korea; alongside other members of the diplomatic corps, heads of institutions, government representatives, international delegates and leading figures in the creative industry. We want to build a platform that places Lagos firmly on the global cultural map, gives African stories the international visibility they deserve and creates meaningful opportunities for our artists. Welcoming over 20,000 attendees, presenting more than 25 productions and bringing international performers from four countries to Lagos is a powerful affirmation of this vision. Theatre is not just entertainment; it is an instrument of cultural identity, economic opportunity and global influence. The Stage Is Everywhere, and Africa must claim its rightful place on that stage.” A Week Of Culture And Collaboration The festival opened on November 9 with Theatre Meets Food at Kaly Restaurant, featuring celebrated chef Hilda Baci in a unique fusion of culinary artistry and live performance. The week also featured diplomatic and cultural engagements hosted by the United States Consul General in Lagos and the British Embassy, alongside a networking reception organised by the British Council for festival directors and participating production companies. These engagements highlighted the importance of international partnerships and cultural diplomacy in advancing Nigeria’s creative industry. Food, beverage and lifestyle brands also contributed to the festival atmosphere, extending the experience beyond the stage. Reflecting on the achievement, Vanessa Jev, Festival Director, said: “This year’s festival demonstrated what is possible when artistic vision, strong partnerships and collective commitment come together. Welcoming over 20,000 attendees, presenting more than 25 productions and hosting international participants from four countries required months of planning and the dedication of an exceptional team. We are proud to have created a platform where Nigerian and international artists could share their work, connect with new audiences and build lasting relationships. This success provides a stronger foundation for expanding the festival’s reach and creating greater opportunities for the creative community.” LITF 2026 gratefully acknowledges its sponsors: Afreximbank, Waltersmith, Pillar Oil, LEDCO, Prime Atlantic, Nigerian Bottling Company, MTN and Wema Bank, whose generous support contributed to the success of the festival. The festival also appreciates its partners : United States Consulate, British Deputy High Commission, British Council, Amstel Malta, Kaly, Beat FM, Classic FM, Smooth FM, Avis, Channels TV, BellaNaija, Africa Movie Channel, My Lagos App, Cadbury and Pulse for their invaluable collaboration and support. Looking Ahead The successful conclusion of LITF 2026 marks another important milestone in the festival’s ambition to position Lagos as a leading destination for theatre and performing arts in Africa. With growing audience engagement, international participation and institutional partnerships, LITF remains committed to showcasing exceptional talent, promoting cultural exchange and building a sustainable global platform for African storytelling. LITF 2026 — THE STAGE IS EVERYWHERE. About LITF The Lagos International Theatre Festival is an annual celebration of theatre, storytelling and artistic expression, bringing together local and international productions, performers and creative professionals. Through performances, cultural engagements and industry collaborations, LITF promotes artistic excellence, encourages cultural exchange and supports the growth of the performing arts industry, with a vision to position Lagos as a leading theatre destination in Africa. item.title: From Dancehall to Rumba, Rema Stretches His Sound on New EP “E-Mortal Boy (EMB)” | Listen
item.description: Rema releases his seven-track EP, E-Mortal Boy (EMB), featuring Wizkid, Theodora, BNYX, and Kah-Lo. Photo Credit: Rema/Instagram For weeks, Rema has been teasing us with a new project—first came “ TEA ” and then “ Oh No “, and if you have had those on repeat on your playlist, you now have the entire package with his seven-track EP, E-Mortal Boy ( EMB ). Ever since his self-titled debut EP in 2019, the Benin-born star has never been interested in staying boxed into one sound. Following his 2023 EP Ravage and his 2024 Grammy-nominated album HEIS , he uses this new seven-song collection to pull rhythms from across the Black diaspora into one bold, genre-hopping ride. If you already had “TEA” on loop when its dancehall bounce, glossy pop, and techno twists took over the Nigerian timeline, or kept “Oh No” close for that percussion-heavy Rvssian groove about a lover’s mixed signals, they both sit right inside the full lineup alongside five more records . The biggest headline moment opens the project: “ Feel Alright ” pairs Rema with Wizkid for their very first official joint release, a smooth ballad about satisfying a lover’s appetite. From there, he switches gears across “ Velvet “, where rumba drums meet slick guitar riffs as he vows to take on the world for someone special, and “ TANZANIA “, a BNYX-assisted track with Bollywood score-inspired flair. The rest of the EP keeps that same adventurous streak alive. On “ SUGA “, Rema teams up with French Congolese singer Theodora for a rougher, grunge-leaning sound, before closing out on “ Bang Bang ” with longtime collaborator London and Nigerian dance music favourite Kah-Lo . Nearly a decade into his run, Rema still sounds completely locked in on what comes next, leaving you with seven quick tracks to drop straight into your weekend rotation. Listen below ﻿ The post From Dancehall to Rumba, Rema Stretches His Sound on New EP “E-Mortal Boy (EMB)” | Listen appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Raye Tops the 2027 Grammy Nominations With 11 Including Album of the Year
item.description: Raye singing on stage with her band and backing vocalists. Photo Credit: Raye/Instagram When the 2027 Grammy nominations dropped earlier this week, one name sat right at the top of the entire board: Raye . Out of every artist in the running for the 69th Annual Grammy Awards, she has the highest Grammy nominations this year with 11 nods, putting her ahead of Rosalía on nine. If you have been watching her rise over the past few years, seeing her command this much spotlight on music’s biggest stage feels well earned, especially for readers following global talent with Ghanaian roots through her mother’s side of the family. Her reaction online captured just how surreal the moment felt, writing on Instagram: “WHAT IS HAPPENING WHAT IS HAPPENING 11 GRAMMY NOMINATIONS INCLUDING ALBUM OF THE YEAR MY HEARTTTTT CANNOT EVEN FATHOM, MY HEARTTTTTTTT ” before following up with a simple “can’t stop crying .” Raye at home with her parents following the 2027 Grammy nominations announcement. Photo Credit: Raye/Instagram In case you are still catching up on her story, Raye was born Rachel Keen in London to a Ghanaian-Swiss mother and an English father, and she has spent years building a reputation as a sharp songwriter, vocalist, and arranger who refuses to stay boxed into one sound. Many listeners first got to know her through chart-topping collaborations and pop hooks before she parted ways with her former major label to release music independently, taking full creative control of her catalogue and storytelling. That independent leap paid off massively—her album This Music May Contain Hope topped the UK chart in March 2026 and won the 2026 Mercury Prize in October, turning her into one of the most talked-about voices in music. Artwork for This Music May Contain Hope. Photo Credit: Raye/Instagram Her 11 nominations for 2027 stretch right across her artistry, from songwriting and performance to arrangement, visuals, and full-length projects. This Music May Contain Hope is competing in both Album of the Year and Best Pop Vocal Album, while her hit “ WHERE IS MY HUSBAND! “—which reached UK No. 1 in January 2026—is up for Record of the Year, Song of the Year, and Best Pop Solo Performance. She also earned nods for “ Click Clack Symphony ” alongside Hans Zimmer in Best Pop Duo/Group Performance, Best Arrangement, Instrumental and Vocals, and Best Music Video, plus “ Life Boat ” in Best Dance Pop Recording, “ I Hate the Way I Look Today” in Best Traditional Pop Vocal Performance, and a Songwriter of the Year, Non-Classical nod. Raye holding a number one award following a year of UK chart milestones, including “WHERE IS MY HUSBAND!” hitting No. 1 in January 2026 and This Music May Contain Hope topping the UK chart in March 2026. Photo Credit: Raye/Instagram This is not her first time on the Grammy radar, though it is easily her biggest moment yet. Before this sweep, Raye had four prior Grammy nominations—taking her career total to 15—including Best New Artist, Songwriter

Photo Credit: Raye/Instagram In case you are still catching up on her story, Raye was born Rachel Keen in London to a Ghanaian-Swiss mother and an English father, and she has spent years building a reputation as a sharp songwriter, vocalist, and arranger who refuses to stay boxed into one sound. Many listeners first got to know her through chart-topping collaborations and pop hooks before she parted ways with her former major label to release music independently, taking full creative control of her catalogue and storytelling. That independent leap paid off massively—her album This Music May Contain Hope topped the UK chart in March 2026 and won the 2026 Mercury Prize in October, turning her into one of the most talked-about voices in music. Artwork for This Music May Contain Hope. Photo Credit: Raye/Instagram Her 11 nominations for 2027 stretch right across her artistry, from songwriting and performance to arrangement, visuals, and full-length projects. This Music May Contain Hope is competing in both Album of the Year and Best Pop Vocal Album, while her hit “ WHERE IS MY HUSBAND! “—which reached UK No. 1 in January 2026—is up for Record of the Year, Song of the Year, and Best Pop Solo Performance. She also earned nods for “ Click Clack Symphony ” alongside Hans Zimmer in Best Pop Duo/Group Performance, Best Arrangement, Instrumental and Vocals, and Best Music Video, plus “ Life Boat ” in Best Dance Pop Recording, “ I Hate the Way I Look Today” in Best Traditional Pop Vocal Performance, and a Songwriter of the Year, Non-Classical nod. Raye holding a number one award following a year of UK chart milestones, including “WHERE IS MY HUSBAND!” hitting No. 1 in January 2026 and This Music May Contain Hope topping the UK chart in March 2026. Photo Credit: Raye/Instagram This is not her first time on the Grammy radar, though it is easily her biggest moment yet. Before this sweep, Raye had four prior Grammy nominations—taking her career total to 15—including Best New Artist, Songwriter of the Year, Non-Classical, and Best Engineered Album, Non-Classical in 2025, plus Best Music Film in 2026 for Live at the Royal Albert Hall. While the Recording Academy previously honoured her with the noncompetitive Harry Belafonte Best Song for Social Change Award for her songwriting on “ Ice Cream Man “, she has never won a competitive Grammy. With 11 chances coming up at the 2027 ceremony on February 7, 2027, we will all be watching to see if she finally brings home her first competitive win—or a whole shelf of them. Raye leads the 2027 Grammy nominations with 11 nods across categories including Album of the Year, Record of the Year, and Song of the Year. Photo Credit: Raye/Instagram The post Raye Tops the 2027 Grammy Nominations With 11 Including Album of the Year appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: A Safari, a Beach & Easy Entry? 5 African Spots for Your Christmas Holiday
item.description: Five African destinations Nigerian passport holders can visit visa-free or with visa on arrival this Christmas holiday. Image: AI-generated. The group chat has the concerts, the dinners and the Detty December link-ups covered. But has anyone planned the getaway? Beyond the usual Lagos parties and end-of-year outings, there is a whole continent waiting to be explored, with sun-soaked beaches, wildlife safaris, exciting food scenes and cities with plenty of stories to tell. You do not have to spend weeks navigating embassy appointments and visa applications to make it happen, either. Several African countries offer Nigerian passport holders visa-free entry or visas on arrival, making a festive-season escape much easier to plan. Whether you are travelling solo, gathering your friends, taking the family along or joining a curated travel group, here are five destinations worth considering for your Christmas holiday. Kenya Imagine spotting lions and giraffes against a city skyline before breakfast, then catching an evening flight or train straight to the coast for fresh seafood by the Indian Ocean. That contrast is what makes Kenya such a rewarding December escape. Nairobi gives you immediate access to wildlife at Nairobi National Park and the Giraffe Centre alongside lively restaurants and art spaces in Westlands and Karen, while longer itineraries open up classic game drives in the Maasai Mara, views of Mount Kilimanjaro in Amboseli, and warm beach days in Diani or Watamu. Nigerian citizens enjoy visa-free entry for short stays of up to 60 days without needing a paid eTA, leaving more room in your budget for safaris and coastal stays. Rwanda Not everyone wants their year-end holiday to feel like a non-stop sprint, and Rwanda is built for travellers who prefer scenery, clean air, and an unhurried pace. Days in Kigali easily revolve around specialty coffee shops, contemporary art at Inema Arts Center, and a sobering, essential visit to the Kigali Genocide Memorial before you head out into the countryside. From the capital, you can track chimpanzees and walk above the trees in Nyungwe Forest, go on wildlife drives in Akagera National Park, or spend quiet afternoons along the shores of Lake Kivu. With 30-day visa-free entry for Nigerian passport holders, getting there is straightforward from start to finish. Between beach days, the bustling Central Market in Port Louis, the lush trails of Black River Gorges National Park, and Casela Nature Parks keep a week-long itinerary full without ever feeling hectic.
